title: World patterns and differences within countries

blocks.heading: World patterns and differences within countries
blocks.text: Development varies across the world and within individual countries. Broad historical patterns place many higher-income industrial economies in Europe, North America and parts of East Asia, while many lower-income economies are found in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia. These are broad geographical patterns, not a current classification list or a claim about every country in a continent. High-income economies also occur outside those regions. Differences within a country can be large: an urban area may have a hospital and reliable water while a remote community has neither. A national average cannot locate those differences.

blocks.heading: Developed, developing, LEDC and MEDC
blocks.text: Developed and developing describe relative levels of development in a simplified way. More developed economies commonly have higher average incomes and wider access to services, but deprivation can persist in them. Developing covers countries with very different resources and experiences; it does not mean that nothing has developed. LEDC means less economically developed country and MEDC means more economically developed country. The economic emphasis matters. A higher income grouping does not show whether rights are protected, water is safe or income is shared equally. Use a label to introduce a comparison, then support that comparison with the indicator that actually answers the question.

blocks.heading: Industrialised and less industrialised economies
blocks.text: Industrialisation is growth in the importance and capacity of industrial production within an economy. Industrialised describes an economy with substantial industrial capacity; less industrialised describes relatively less. The existence of one factory does not settle the classification. Industrialisation can expand production, paid work and opportunities to learn technical skills. Its effect on living standards also depends on wages, safety, access to those jobs and environmental damage. An economy with a large service sector may still have substantial industrial capacity. Economic structure and quality of life are related questions, but neither is a complete substitute for the other.

blocks.heading: Capitalism and communism
blocks.text: Capitalism emphasises private ownership of productive resources and market decisions about production and exchange. Communism as an economic ideal involves common ownership of productive resources; economies described as communist have generally relied heavily on state ownership and central planning. These descriptions concern ownership and decision making. They are not names for rich and poor. In practice, an economy may combine private shops, state services and public regulation. Establish the ownership arrangement from the evidence rather than assigning a development level from its label. Political institutions and economic arrangements also need to be examined separately.

blocks.heading: Newly industrialised countries
blocks.text: A newly industrialised country, or NIC, has undergone substantial, relatively recent industrial expansion and structural change. Manufacturing and industrial employment become more important. The term is used in historical accounts of development and has no single permanent membership list. For this topic, understand the change the term describes rather than memorising a supposed up-to-date list. Expanding industry may create employment and exports while some households remain poor. To describe development, ask about the effects on income and living conditions as well as the change in production.

blocks.heading: Reading an original comparison
blocks.text: In a fictional same-year comparison, Region A has income per person of N$90,000 and 95% safe-water access; Region B has N$25,000 and 60% access. Region A combines higher average income with wider water access: income is N$65,000 higher and access is 35 percentage points higher. Those two observations support a difference in both economic resources and a living-condition indicator. They do not establish the political system or prove that income caused water access. A figure describes what was measured. A relationship links relevant figures without claiming more than they establish.

blocks.heading: Keep classifications separate
blocks.text: Topic 4.1 develops industrialisation and its consequences. The indicators in the next lesson give evidence for comparing development. When reading a source, first identify whether its labels concern income, industry or ownership. Then choose evidence relevant to the comparison. This avoids treating all three classifications as interchangeable.
